item.text: I’m reviewing the earlier scope from memory only and will save only additional rows to `followup.tsv`, keeping references and connections distinct from the prior proposals.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/103_2/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.90.11	finite lifespan, toil and swift passing	The psalm numbers a human life at seventy or eighty years, marked by toil, then says it passes quickly; this develops the commentary's time-as-principal image into a lifespan.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.90.11	עמל (table sound correspondence; unverified)	The commentary's neighboring وَعَمِلُوا۟ names good action; this verse says human years are עָמָל and trouble before they fly away. The table's Arabic ع م ل–Hebrew עמל correspondence is unverified, while the shared labor context is explicit.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.49.19	wealth cannot follow its owner in death	The rich person takes nothing when he dies and his glory does not descend after him; this matches the commentary's claim that accumulated capital cannot save the person who spent it.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.5.15	nothing carried from birth or toil	A person leaves as naked as he came and cannot take the fruit of his labor; this supplies a direct account of worldly gain failing at death.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.23.4	stop striving to acquire wealth	Proverbs warns against wearing oneself out to get rich; this directly questions the commentary's merchant-like pursuit of gain as a use of finite human time.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.23.5	wealth grows wings and vanishes	The wealth a person fixes his eyes on suddenly makes wings and flies away; the image makes visible the commentary's principal that disappears despite apparent accumulation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.17.11	unjust wealth abandoned midlife	One who gains wealth unjustly is likened to a bird hatching what it did not lay and will leave it in midlife; this joins fraudulent gain to the loss of the person who thought it secure.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.4	riches fail on the day of wrath	Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; this contrasts market capital with what can answer at final judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.2.3	God weighs deeds	Hannah says the Lord is a God of knowledge and actions are weighed by him; this links the commentary's unseen human account to divine assessment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.11	balances belong to the Lord	The verse says just balances and weights are the Lord's work; this joins the commentary's fair market scale to divine order and judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.10	wicked stores and short measure	Micah asks whether wicked treasure remains in a house with a scant measure; the prophet links stored wealth to the short measure that the commentary describes as stealing another's principal.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.11	false balances under divine judgment	The Lord asks whether he can acquit someone with wicked scales and deceptive weights; this makes the dishonest trader's reduced measure answerable to judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.7.2	worker longs for shade and wages	Job compares the sufferer to a slave longing for shade and a hired worker waiting for wages; this continues the commentary's connection between human time, labor and its due.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.7.3	months of emptiness appointed	Job says months of emptiness and nights of misery have been allotted to him; the verse gives a concrete example of living inside loss as an extended condition.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.14.6	a person's allotted day as a hireling's	Job asks God to turn away until a person's day, like that of a hired worker, is complete; this links the commentary's due term to the end of labor and life.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Eccl.9.2	righteous and wicked share one fate	Qohelet says the same event happens to righteous and wicked alike; this counters the commentary's exception group at the level of earthly outcomes, without directly addressing its afterlife account.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.3	fruitful tree that does not wither	The righteous person is a tree bearing fruit in season whose leaf does not wither; this contrasts the commentary's crop lost to a destructive wind with a life that remains productive.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.4	wicked as windblown chaff	The wicked are like chaff driven away by wind; this gives a scriptural contrast between the fruitful life and the commentary's image of a life's produce swept away.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.19	fruitless tree cut down and burned	Jesus says a tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this joins the commentary's produce imagery to judgment based on what a life yields.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.12.36	account for every careless word	Jesus says people will give account on judgment day for every careless word; this makes the commentary's comprehensive human reckoning concrete down to speech.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	dead judged from books by their works	At the great throne, the dead are judged from opened books according to their works; this is a direct image of the final account that the commentary hears behind loss and deeds.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.9.27	death followed by judgment	The verse says humans die once and afterward face judgment; it fits the commentary's image of each person reaching a fixed term and being assessed.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.25	postmortem reversal of rich and poor	Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, and now their conditions are reversed; this shows status and present comfort do not settle the final account.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.16.6	steward reduces a debt by half	The steward changes an oil debtor's bill from one hundred measures to fifty; unlike the commentary's condemned short measure, the parable places debt reduction inside a crisis strategy for future welcome.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.16.8	dishonest steward praised for prudence	The master praises the dishonest steward's foresight, not his dishonesty; this complicates the commentary's pairing of financial manipulation and loss by distinguishing prudent use of wealth from moral accounting.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Luke.17.33	preserving life leads to losing it	Jesus says whoever seeks to preserve life will lose it, while whoever loses it will keep it; this gives a distinct saying in which self-protection reverses into the commentary's loss of self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.7	former gains counted as loss	Paul says the things that were gain to him he counted as loss for Christ; the accounting language directly meets the commentary's distinction between apparent assets and true profit.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.8	all things loss for the greater gain	Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him; this adds a deliberate revaluation in which relinquishing worldly capital is itself gain.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.7	nothing brought in or carried out	Paul says people bring nothing into the world and can take nothing out; this directly undercuts the assumption that accumulated wealth can secure the self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.9	desire for riches plunges people into ruin	Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and destructive desires; this connects pursuit of wealth to the commentary's loss of health, faith and self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.2	stored wealth decays	James says the rich person's wealth has rotted and garments have been eaten by moths; this gives physical form to the commentary's claim that capital can diminish while held.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.3	rust testifies against wealth	Gold and silver rust becomes evidence against their owners and consumes them like fire; the verse links hoarding to a coming reckoning and adds a fire image to the commentary's crop-loss scene.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Matt.13.44	joyful sale for a greater treasure	The finder sells everything to buy the field with hidden treasure; this reverses the commentary's loss account by showing a total expenditure that is profitable because the acquired good is greater.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.1.3	work of faith and steadfast hope	Paul remembers the community's work of faith, labor of love and steadfastness of hope; this is a specific Christian formulation of faith joined to action and endurance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.17	faith without works is dead	James says faith by itself, without works, is dead; this closely matches the commentary's neighboring exception, where belief is joined to righteous action.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hab.2.4	righteous live by faith	In the vision's contrast between the proud and the upright, the righteous live by faith; this gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's group whose faith keeps them from loss.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Rom.1.17	Paul rereads Habakkuk as gospel principle	Paul quotes Habakkuk's righteous-by-faith line as the revelation of God's righteousness in the gospel; this Christian reading emphasizes faith as the principle of life alongside the commentary's fuller faith-and-deeds description.
strong	incil	motif	Didache 1.1	two ways, life and death	The Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death; this gives a concrete early Christian form to the commentary's secondary sense of loss as leaving the right path.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 1:14	self, community and the urgency of now	Hillel asks who one is if wholly for oneself and, if not now, when; the saying joins the commentary's isolated human, mutual counsel and finite time.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:4	do not separate from the community	The Mishnah warns against separating from the community, trusting oneself until death, or postponing study until free; this connects collective support and urgency to the commentary's path out of isolation and loss.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 3:1	account before the Judge	Akavya ben Mahalalel tells a person to know where he came from and where he goes, and before whom he will give account; this is a direct Jewish formulation of the commentary's human life reaching its reckoning.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	Mishnah Avot 4:1	wealth redefined as contentment	Ben Zoma asks who is rich and answers: one who rejoices in his portion; this challenges the commentary's market image by defining wealth through sufficiency rather than accumulation.
strong	tevrat	motif	Kiddushin 40b	one deed tips the moral scales	The Talmud asks each person to see himself as balanced between merit and guilt, so one deed can tip himself and the world; this is a close rabbinic meeting of human action, scales and final consequence.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Rosh Hashanah 16b	people inscribed by their deeds at the New Year	The Talmud describes books opened on the New Year and distinguishes the righteous, wicked and intermediate by their inscription for life or death; this gives the commentary's universal verdict and exception group a Jewish judgment-day framework.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.23.2	חסר (table sound correspondence; unverified)	The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; the Hebrew speaker says לֹא אֶחְסָר, “I lack nothing,” within the shepherd's provision. The table's sound correspondence is unverified, and the verse supplies a precise counter-image of sufficiency.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.51.12	אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)	The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Isaiah asks why anyone fears אֱנוֹשׁ, a mortal who dies and is like grass. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while the verse adds human mortality and fear.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Jer.15.18	אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)	The source's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ is linked in the table to Hebrew אנש; Jeremiah calls his wound אָנֻשָׁה, incurable. This is the root's illness/weakness usage, not a claim that the Arabic noun means illness.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.1.4	צבר (table sound correspondence; unverified)	The commentary's neighboring صَبْر names endurance, while Psalm 1 calls the wicked chaff driven by wind, using the table-linked צבר consonants only as a candidate. The verse's windblown instability is the contextual bridge; the sound match does not establish cognacy.
EOF"

strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.17.33	preserving life leads to losing it	Jesus says whoever seeks to preserve life will lose it, while whoever loses it will keep it; this gives a distinct saying in which self-protection reverses into the commentary's loss of self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.7	former gains counted as loss	Paul says the things that were gain to him he counted as loss for Christ; the accounting language directly meets the commentary's distinction between apparent assets and true profit.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.8	all things loss for the greater gain	Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him; this adds a deliberate revaluation in which relinquishing worldly capital is itself gain.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.7	nothing brought in or carried out	Paul says people bring nothing into the world and can take nothing out; this directly undercuts the assumption that accumulated wealth can secure the self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.9	desire for riches plunges people into ruin	Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and destructive desires; this connects pursuit of wealth to the commentary's loss of health, faith and self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.2	stored wealth decays	James says the rich person's wealth has rotted and garments have been eaten by moths; this gives physical form to the commentary's claim that capital can diminish while held.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.3	rust testifies against wealth	Gold and silver rust becomes evidence against their owners and consumes them like fire; the verse links hoarding to a coming reckoning and adds a fire image to the commentary's crop-loss scene.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Matt.13.44	joyful sale for a greater treasure	The finder sells everything to buy the field with hidden treasure; this reverses the commentary's loss account by showing a total expenditure that is profitable because the acquired good is greater.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.1.3	work of faith and steadfast hope	Paul remembers the community's work of faith, labor of love and steadfastness of hope; this is a specific Christian formulation of faith joined to action and endurance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.17	faith without works is dead	James says faith by itself, without works, is dead; this closely matches the commentary's neighboring exception, where belief is joined to righteous action.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hab.2.4	righteous live by faith	In the vision's contrast between the proud and the upright, the righteous live by faith; this gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's group whose faith keeps them from loss.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Rom.1.17	Paul rereads Habakkuk as gospel principle	Paul quotes Habakkuk's righteous-by-faith line as the revelation of God's righteousness in the gospel; this Christian reading emphasizes faith as the principle of life alongside the commentary's fuller faith-and-deeds description.
medium	incil	motif	Didache 1.1	two ways, life and death	The Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death; this gives a concrete early Christian form to the commentary's secondary sense of loss as leaving the right path.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 1:14	self, community and the urgency of now	Hillel asks who one is if wholly for oneself and, if not now, when; the saying joins the commentary's isolated human, mutual counsel and finite time.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:4	do not separate from the community	The Mishnah warns against separating from the community, trusting oneself until death, or postponing study until free; this connects collective support and urgency to the commentary's path out of isolation and loss.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 3:1	account before the Judge	Akavya ben Mahalalel tells a person to know where he came from and where he goes, and before whom he will give account; this is a direct Jewish formulation of the commentary's human life reaching its reckoning.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	Mishnah Avot 4:1	wealth redefined as contentment	Ben Zoma asks who is rich and answers: one who rejoices in his portion; this challenges the commentary's market image by defining wealth through sufficiency rather than accumulation.
strong	tevrat	motif	Kiddushin 40b	one deed tips the moral scales	The Talmud asks each person to see himself as balanced between merit and guilt, so one deed can tip himself and the world; this is a close rabbinic meeting of human action, scales and final consequence.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Rosh Hashanah 16b	people inscribed by their deeds at the New Year	The Talmud describes books opened on the New Year and distinguishes the righteous, wicked and intermediate by their inscription for life or death; this gives the commentary's universal verdict and exception group a Jewish judgment-day framework.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.23.2	חסר (table sound correspondence; unverified)	The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; the Hebrew speaker says לֹא אֶחְסָר, “I lack nothing,” within the shepherd's provision. medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.51.12	אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)	The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Isaiah asks why anyone fears אֱנוֹשׁ, a mortal who dies and is like grass. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while the verse adds human mortality and fear.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Jer.15.18	אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)	The source's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ is linked in the table to Hebrew אנש; Jeremiah calls his wound אָנֻשָׁה, incurable. This is the root's illness/weakness usage, not a claim that the Arabic noun means illness.
